content: Polysaccharides are complex carbohydrates composed of numerous monosaccharide units linked together by glycosidic bonds. These macromolecules are typically large and often branched. They are generally amorphous, insoluble in water, and lack a sweet taste. When all the monosaccharides in a polysaccharide are of the same type, the molecule is classified as a homopolysaccharide. Conversely, if more than one type of monosaccharide is present, it is referred to as a heteropolysaccharide. Examples of polysaccharides include storage forms such as starch and glycogen, as well as structural forms like cellulose and chitin. The general chemical formula for polysaccharides is Cn(H2O)n-1, where n is typically a large number ranging from 200 to 2500. For polymers composed of six-carbon monosaccharides, the formula can also be represented as (C6H10O5)n, where n ranges from 40 to 3000. Storage Polysaccharides Starches Starches are glucose polymers in which glucopyranose units are connected by alpha-linkages. They consist of a mixture of two components: amylose and amylopectin. Amylose is a linear chain of several hundred glucose molecules, while amylopectin is a branched molecule containing several thousand glucose units. Starches are insoluble in water and can be broken down through hydrolysis, a process catalyzed by enzymes known as amylases. These enzymes cleave the alpha-linkages (glycosidic bonds) in starch. Humans and other animals possess amylases, enabling them to digest starches. Common dietary sources of starch include potatoes, rice, wheat, and maize. Structural Polysaccharides Cellulose Cellulose is a primary structural component of plants. It is a polymer composed of repeated glucose units linked by beta-linkages. Wood is primarily made of cellulose and lignin, while paper and cotton are nearly pure cellulose. Humans and many other animals lack the enzyme required to break beta-linkages, rendering cellulose indigestible. However, certain animals, such as termites, can digest cellulose due to the presence of gut bacteria that produce the necessary enzyme. Acidic Polysaccharides Acidic polysaccharides are characterized by the presence of carboxyl groups, phosphate groups, and/or sulfuric ester groups within their structure. Bacterial Capsule Polysaccharides Pathogenic bacteria often produce a thick, mucous-like layer of polysaccharide known as a capsule. This capsule conceals antigenic proteins on the bacterial surface, preventing immune recognition and destruction. Capsular polysaccharides are water-soluble, typically acidic, and have molecular weights ranging from 100 to 1000 kDa. They are linear and consist of regularly repeating subunits composed of one to six monosaccharides. There is significant structural diversity among these polysaccharides; for instance, Escherichia coli alone produces nearly 200 different types. Mixtures of capsular polysaccharides, either in their native form or conjugated, are used in vaccine development. Bacteria and other microbes, including fungi and algae, often secrete polysaccharides as an evolutionary adaptation to adhere to surfaces and prevent desiccation. Humans have utilized some of these microbial polysaccharides, such as xanthan gum, dextran, gellan gum, and pullulan, for various applications. Cell-surface polysaccharides play diverse roles in bacterial physiology. They act as a barrier between the cell wall and the environment, mediate host-pathogen interactions, and contribute to the structural integrity of biofilms. These polysaccharides are synthesized from nucleotide-activated precursors, and the genes encoding the enzymes required for their biosynthesis, assembly, and transport are typically organized into dedicated clusters within the bacterial genome. Lipopolysaccharides are among the most critical cell-surface polysaccharides, as they are essential for maintaining the structural integrity of the outer membrane and mediating host-pathogen interactions. The genetics underlying the biosynthesis of homopolymeric (A-band) and heteropolymeric (B-band) O antigens have been well-characterized, and significant progress has been made in elucidating the biochemical pathways involved in their synthesis. The exopolysaccharide alginate is a linear copolymer of β-1,4-linked D-mannuronic acid and L-guluronic acid residues. It is responsible for the mucoid phenotype observed in late-stage cystic fibrosis disease. Additionally, the recently discovered pel and psl loci encode exopolysaccharides that are critical for biofilm formation. Rhamnolipid, a biosurfactant, is tightly regulated at the transcriptional level, although its precise role in disease remains poorly understood. Protein glycosylation, particularly of pilin and flagellin, has emerged as a significant area of research. This process has been shown to be crucial for bacterial adhesion and invasion during infection.
